chunks: Calibrate, validate and test a sensor. The question: How do you calibrate/validate/test a sensor? Describe what you would want to test and design an experiment.
Three different jobs are bundled here. Calibrating a sensor means comparing it with a trusted reference and finding a correction for its steady errors.
Validating means proving the correction works on data you did not use to build it.
Testing means stressing the sensor in the conditions it will really face, such as heat, supply changes and vibration.
Think of a bathroom scale. To calibrate it, you place known weights on it and adjust until it agrees.
To validate it, you try a weight you did not use for adjusting and see whether it still reads right.
To test it, you check it on a cold floor, after a bump, or with a weak battery. Checking only with the weights you adjusted it with would look perfect and prove little.
The loop to remember is fit, check on held-out data, and if the residual shows a pattern, add a model term (or fix the setup) before touching the sensor.
Stress tests come after the model is trustworthy.
Reference: an instrument much more accurate than the sensor under test, ideally at least four times better. Offset and gain: offset is the error when the true input is zero.
Gain error is a wrong scale factor. Residual: what remains after correction, the corrected reading minus the reference.
Held-out data: measurements not used in the fit, saved for the check. Hysteresis: reading depends on whether you approached from above or below.
A sensor reads 0. 20 when the true input is 0, and 11. 10 when it is 10. The gain is (11. 10 minus 0. 20) divided by 10, which is 1. 09. The offset is 0. 20.
The correction is true value equals reading minus 0. 20, all divided by 1. 09. Now check at a true input of 5, a point not used in the fit. The sensor reads 5.
55, and the corrected value is 4. 908. That is off by 0. 092: two points fixed offset and gain, but not the curve in the middle (nonlinearity). That is the whole idea.
"Calibration fixes the systematic error against a reference that's at least four times better than the sensor: offset and gain at minimum, more points if it's nonlinear.
Validation checks that correction on points I did not fit, across range and temperature, against the spec. Testing stresses it with supply changes, warm-up, vibration and noise.
My experiment is a sweep up and down over the full range with many samples per point, a fit on half the points and a check on the other half, repeated on several units.
That separates bias, noise, hysteresis and unit-to-unit spread."
Quick check. Which activity checks that a correction works on data that was NOT used to compute the correction?
